desc:
A service stores accounts as integer rows. Each row is [owner, email1, email2, ...]: the first number is the id of the account's owner and the remaining numbers are the (positive integer) email ids registered on that account. An email may be listed twice inside one row.

Two accounts belong to the same person if they share at least one email, directly or through a chain of other accounts (A shares with B, B shares with C, so all three are one person). Different people can have the same owner id, so equal owner ids alone never justify a merge. It is guaranteed that accounts sharing an email also have the same owner id.

Merge the accounts of each person into one row: the owner id first, followed by all distinct emails of that person in increasing order. Return the merged rows sorted lexicographically (compare row elements from left to right, a shorter row that is a prefix of another comes first).

accounts = [[1,10,20],[2,30],[1,20,40],[1,50]]
-> [[1,10,20,40],[1,50],[2,30]]
accounts = [[7,3,1],[7,2],[7,4,2],[7,5,4]]
-> [[7,1,3],[7,2,4,5]]
constraints: Each row has at least 2 numbers (an owner and at least one email), and at most 10 emails
Two accounts that share an email have the same owner id
hints: Accounts are the vertices of a graph; two accounts are linked when they share an email. Each person is a connected component.
Walk through the accounts and remember, for each email, the first account where you saw it. Every later account holding that email must be merged with that first account.

Union the account indices with union-find using that email-to-first-account map. Afterwards collect the emails of every account into a set for its root, sort each set, put the owner first, and sort all rows.
editorial: Treat every account index as a node of a union-find structure. Scan all accounts and keep a dictionary first[email]. If the email was seen before, union the current account with first[email]; otherwise record the current account. After this pass, two accounts are in the same set exactly when they are linked through a chain of shared emails.

Then group: for every account add its emails to a set belonging to its root (the owner id is the same for the whole group). Output [owner] + sorted(emails) for each group and sort the list of rows. With E total emails the cost is O(E α) for the unions plus O(E log E) for sorting. A DFS over an email-to-accounts graph gives the same result.
